interactions.summary: Students extend Jiang's self-authored-weight model by suggesting that damnation comes from failing to forgive oneself, that God's action is to draw people toward him and help them shed those weights, and that the real question is whether humans watch God rather than live under divine surveillance.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led classroom exchange with multiple student replies

speaker_notes.note: The ASR is noisy in the middle of this reply, but the student appears to be linking guilt or innocence to whether one senses God's presence.

claims.claim: A student proposes that the deepest burden is self-unforgiveness: some people could forgive themselves but believe their sins are too great for that release.
Jiang presses the class to say explicitly that God's action is not punishment but some positive attempt to move human beings toward him.
A student answers that if people put the weights on themselves, then God is trying to tell them to take those weights off.
Jiang crystallizes the point by saying God is like a tractor beam that has locked onto you and is trying to draw you toward him.
Another student tries to shift the picture from divine surveillance to human orientation, asking whether the real agency lies in our watching God rather than God watching us.

signature_moments.moment: The burden of sin is reimagined as an inability to forgive oneself rather than as an external sentence.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It pushes the lecture further toward self-authored damnation and away from punitive theology.

signature_moments.moment: God becomes a tractor beam already locked on to the soul.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: The image makes divine grace an active pull instead of a detached judgment seat.

signature_moments.moment: The decisive surveillance reversal is whether we are the ones watching God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Are we watching God rather than him watching us
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This question sets up Jiang's next explicit model of salvation as chosen orientation.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's science-fiction image for God's constant effort to draw the human being toward him.
A student's explanation for salvation pressure: people remain burdened when they cannot release their own guilt.
Raised here as the question of whether movement toward God depends on our own orientation and attention rather than divine monitoring.

chronology_notes.note: This packet continues the same class-day argument about free will and self-made burden, adding new metaphors for divine attraction rather than a dated shift in Jiang's position.

uncertainty_notes.note: Part of the student's formulation about guilt and God's presence is garbled by ASR, so only the general conscience-oriented gist is safe to retain.
